title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
summary: Ten database concepts every system design candidate must know, from indexing and transactions to replication and sharding. Each one covers what it is, how it works with a concrete example, its trade-offs, and the interview takeaway.

chapters.title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip
points: Cover title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
1. Indexing: find rows without scanning the table
2. Transactions: group statements into one unit of work
3. ACID: the four guarantees a transaction promises
4. Isolation Levels: how much concurrent transactions see of each other
5. MVCC: readers and writers without blocking
6. Locking: serializing conflicting writes
7. Connection Pooling: reuse expensive connections
8. Partitioning: split one big table inside one database
9. Replication: copy data to other nodes for reads and failover
10. Sharding: split data across independent databases
Order runs foundational to advanced; the last page is a one-page cheatsheet

chapters.title: Indexing
points: What it is: a separate sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations
Why it exists: without one, a lookup is a full table scan, O(n); a B-tree lookup is O(log n)
Used for: WHERE filters, JOIN keys, ORDER BY, and enforcing UNIQUE constraints
How it works: table users has 10,000,000 rows; SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='a@x.com' scans every row (about 2 s)
How it works: after CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email) the same query descends about 4 B-tree levels and returns in under 1 ms
Benefit: reads on indexed columns drop from O(n) to O(log n)
Benefit: composite index (country, created_at) serves WHERE country='IN' ORDER BY created_at without a sort
Benefit: a covering index holds every selected column, so the table is never touched (index-only scan)
Consider: every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must also update each index, so writes slow down
Consider: composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule; (a,b) helps WHERE a=1 but not WHERE b=2
Consider: wrapping the column in a function, as in WHERE LOWER(email)=..., skips the index; low-cardinality columns like boolean gain little
Interview takeaway: index for your read patterns, say what it costs on writes, and prove it with EXPLAIN

chapters.title: Transactions
points: What it is: a group of statements that either all take effect (COMMIT) or none do (ROLLBACK)
Why it exists: a crash or error halfway through a multi-step change would otherwise leave data inconsistent
Used for: money transfers, order placement plus stock decrement, any change spanning several rows or tables
How it works: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;
How it works: if the second UPDATE fails, ROLLBACK restores account 1 to its original balance; no money is lost
Benefit: all-or-nothing changes, with no partially applied state visible to others
Benefit: savepoints let you roll back part of a transaction and keep the rest
Consider: long transactions hold locks and block others, and they bloat undo logs
Consider: never call external services (HTTP, email) inside a transaction; the rollback cannot unsend them
Consider: autocommit makes each statement its own transaction, so a two-step change needs an explicit BEGIN
Interview takeaway: keep transactions short, scope them to one logical operation, and name what must be atomic

chapters.title: ACID
points: What it is: four guarantees a transaction system provides: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Why it exists: to make concurrent, crash-prone storage behave predictably for application code
Used for: choosing between relational databases (ACID by default) and some NoSQL stores that relax it
How it works: Atomicity is all-or-nothing, implemented with an undo log
How it works: Consistency means constraints (foreign keys, CHECK balance>=0) hold before and after the commit
How it works: Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work
How it works: Durability means committed data survives a crash, via a write-ahead log (WAL) fsynced at commit
Benefit: example: a transfer of 100 that violates CHECK(balance>=0) is rejected whole, leaving both balances unchanged
Consider: strong ACID costs latency, since the WAL fsync per commit is a disk wait
Consider: ACID is per node; a transaction across shards needs two-phase commit and is much slower
Consider: ACID's C is not the C in CAP; ACID C is rules, CAP C is replica agreement
Interview takeaway: be able to name each letter and its mechanism: undo log, constraints, isolation, WAL

chapters.title: Isolation Levels
points: What it is: a setting that controls which anomalies concurrent transactions may observe
Why it exists: full isolation is slow, so databases let you trade correctness for throughput
Used for: tuning per transaction with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ...
How it works: Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data)
How it works: Read Committed prevents dirty reads; this is the default in PostgreSQL and Oracle
How it works: Repeatable Read also prevents non-repeatable reads; it is the MySQL InnoDB default
How it works: Serializable prevents phantoms and makes the result equal to some serial order
Example: T1 reads balance=500; T2 commits 300; T1 re-reads 300; that is a non-repeatable read under Read Committed
Benefit: lower levels give higher concurrency and fewer aborts
Consider: write skew (two doctors both go off call) can still occur under Repeatable Read or snapshot isolation
Consider: Serializable can abort transactions, so the client must retry on a serialization failure
Interview takeaway: name the anomaly you are guarding against, then choose the weakest level that prevents it

chapters.title: MVCC
points: What it is: Multi-Version Concurrency Control keeps multiple versions of a row so each transaction reads a consistent snapshot
Why it exists: to stop readers blocking writers and writers blocking readers
Used for: PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, and Oracle snapshot reads
How it works: every row version carries creator and deleter transaction IDs (PostgreSQL xmin and xmax)
How it works: example: T100 starts and sees balance=500; T101 updates it to 300 and commits; T100 still reads 500 from its snapshot
How it works: an UPDATE writes a new row version; the old one stays until no snapshot needs it
Benefit: plain reads take no locks, so read-heavy workloads scale
Benefit: gives consistent point-in-time reads, such as for backups and reports
Consider: dead row versions pile up as bloat, and PostgreSQL needs VACUUM to reclaim them
Consider: a long-running transaction pins old versions and blocks cleanup
Consider: MVCC does not stop two writers from updating the same row; writers still conflict
Interview takeaway: say MVCC means readers don't block writers, and name its price: version cleanup

chapters.title: Locking
points: What it is: a mechanism that makes concurrent transactions wait for each other on shared data
Why it exists: two writers changing the same row would otherwise lose an update
Used for: protecting inventory counts, balances, and unique allocations
How it works: shared (S) locks allow many readers; exclusive (X) locks allow one writer
How it works: pessimistic: SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id=7 FOR UPDATE; locks the row until COMMIT
How it works: optimistic: UPDATE items SET stock=9, version=4 WHERE id=7 AND version=3; zero rows updated means retry
Benefit: pessimistic locks stop the lost update, so two buyers cannot both take the last item
Benefit: optimistic locking takes no locks, so it suits low-contention workloads
Consider: deadlock: T1 locks row A then B while T2 locks B then A; the DB aborts one
Consider: lock rows in a consistent order across code paths to avoid deadlocks
Consider: row locks are cheap, but a table lock blocks every other writer
Interview takeaway: choose pessimistic for high contention and optimistic for low, and know how to avoid deadlocks

chapters.title: Connection Pooling
points: What it is: a cache of open database connections that requests borrow and return
Why it exists: opening a connection costs a TCP and TLS handshake plus authentication, often 20-50 ms, and a server process
Used for: web apps, serverless functions, microservices (HikariCP, PgBouncer, pgpool)
How it works: the pool opens 10 connections at startup; a request borrows one, runs its query, and returns it
How it works: example: 500 app threads share a pool of 20; the other 480 wait in a queue, and the DB sees only 20 connections
Benefit: removes per-request connect latency
Benefit: caps concurrent load, protecting the database from connection storms
Benefit: PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes thousands of clients over a few server connections
Consider: PostgreSQL's default max_connections is 100 and each connection uses memory, so size the pool small
Consider: a pool that is too large causes contention, and a good start is about (cores x 2) + disks
Consider: leaked connections (not returned) exhaust the pool; set a timeout and always release in finally
Interview takeaway: a smaller, bounded pool beats a large one; mention PgBouncer for serverless

chapters.title: Partitioning
points: What it is: splitting one large table into smaller physical pieces (partitions) inside a single database
Why it exists: huge tables make queries, indexes, and maintenance slow
Used for: time-series logs, events, and orders that grow forever
How it works: range partitioning by month: orders_2026_01, orders_2026_02, and so on
How it works: example: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01' reads only orders_2026_03; this is partition pruning
How it works: hash partitioning spreads rows evenly by hash(user_id) % 8; list partitioning groups by region
Benefit: pruning cuts I/O, since queries read a fraction of the data
Benefit: dropping an old partition is instant, compared with a slow DELETE of millions of rows
Benefit: indexes per partition stay small and fit in memory
Consider: queries that omit the partition key scan all partitions
Consider: bad key choice creates a hot partition, such as monthly ranges where only the current month is written
Consider: partitioning stays on one machine, so it does not add capacity beyond that server
Interview takeaway: partitioning is within one database; say it before you reach for sharding

chapters.title: Replication
points: What it is: keeping copies of the same data on multiple database nodes
Why it exists: to survive node failure and to scale reads
Used for: read replicas, high availability, cross-region reads, and backups
How it works: single-leader: the primary takes writes and streams its WAL or binlog to followers
How it works: example: 1 primary and 3 replicas; the app sends writes to the primary and spreads SELECTs across the replicas
How it works: if the primary fails, a replica is promoted (failover)
Benefit: read throughput scales roughly with replica count
Benefit: failover cuts downtime from hours to seconds
Consider: asynchronous replication lags, so a user may write and then read stale data from a replica
Consider: synchronous replication has no loss but raises write latency, since it waits for the replica ack
Consider: multi-leader and leaderless setups bring write conflicts that need resolution (last-write-wins, CRDTs)
Consider: replication does not scale writes, since every node applies every write
Interview takeaway: replication gives read scale and availability, and the price is consistency lag

chapters.title: Sharding
points: What it is: splitting data horizontally across independent database servers (shards), each holding a subset of rows
Why it exists: one machine eventually hits its write throughput, storage, or memory limit
Used for: very large systems such as social feeds, messaging, and multi-tenant SaaS
How it works: a shard key decides placement; shard = hash(user_id) % 4 sends user 1001 to shard 1
How it works: range sharding (A-F, G-M) allows range scans but risks hot spots; directory-based lookup is flexible but adds a lookup service
How it works: consistent hashing lets you add a shard and move only about 1/N of the keys
Benefit: scales writes and storage nearly linearly with shard count
Benefit: a fault stays contained, since one shard failing affects only its users
Consider: cross-shard joins and transactions are slow or unsupported, so they need two-phase commit or app logic
Consider: a bad shard key creates hot shards, such as a celebrity user or sequential IDs on one shard
Consider: resharding is painful, so shard late, after indexing, replicas, and partitioning
Interview takeaway: sharding is the last resort; justify the shard key and its cross-shard cost

chapters.title: Cheatsheet: Database Concepts at a Glance
points: Indexing: B-tree turns O(n) scans into O(log n); costs write speed and space
Transactions: BEGIN ... COMMIT or ROLLBACK; keep them short
ACID: undo log for A, constraints for C, isolation for I, WAL for D
Isolation: Read Committed (Postgres default), Repeatable Read (MySQL default), Serializable (strictest)
Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, write skew
MVCC: row versions per snapshot, so readers never block writers; needs VACUUM
Locking: FOR UPDATE (pessimistic) vs version column (optimistic); order locks to avoid deadlock
Connection pool: size about (cores x 2) + disks; PgBouncer for serverless
Partitioning: split one table on one server; pruning needs the partition key in the query
Replication: read scale and failover; async lag means stale reads
Sharding: scale writes across servers; the shard key is the critical choice
Scaling ladder: index, then cache and pool, then replicate, then partition, then shard
